epaPastUses.title: Past Property Uses May Result in a Brownfield Site (U.S. EPA, 2024)

FUEL.label: Fuel tanks and filling stations
possibleContaminants: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and solvents used for cleaning and repair
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) from asphalt and combustion
questions: Ask the seller or the state environmental agency whether any underground storage tanks were registered, removed or closed at or near this address.
Ask whether a Phase I environmental site assessment has been done for the property.
Check your state's leaking underground storage tank (LUST) list for nearby addresses.

AUTO.label: Garages and auto repair
possibleContaminants: Petroleum from fuels, spills and past fuel storage
PAHs from combustion, asphalt, ash and fill
Lead and other metals from paint and radiator solder
questions: Ask whether a Phase I environmental site assessment has been done for the property.
Ask whether the old garage had fuel tanks or floor drains, and whether they were removed.

INDUSTRIAL.label: Industry and workshops
possibleContaminants: Lead from paint on structures and equipment
Petroleum and fuel for equipment and heating
PAHs from power generation, burning, ash and fill
Other metals, solvents and hazardous substances from manufacturing
questions: Ask whether a Phase I environmental site assessment has been done for the property.
Ask the local planning or environmental office what is on record for the old industrial site.

RAIL.label: Railroad lines and yards
possibleContaminants: Lead from paint on old structures, equipment and railcars
Other metals from railcar repair and the treatment of wooden ties
PAHs from coal and diesel combustion, ash and fill
Pesticides or herbicides used for weed control
questions: Ask whether a Phase I environmental site assessment has been done for the property.
Ask whether fill soil near the old rail line was ever tested before gardening or building.

disclaimer: These are historical leads from old maps, not findings. Map placement is usually accurate to about 10 feet but is sometimes wrong. Only an environmental assessment or testing can show whether a site is contaminated.
